blocks.text: Hyponatraemia is defined as a serum sodium concentration below 135 mmol/L.

blocks.title: Sodium is the major extracellular cation and plays an essential role in:

items.text: Regulation of water distribution between intracellular and extracellular compartments.

blocks.text: Hyponatraemia occurs when there is an excess of water relative to sodium in the body.
It is particularly important because a rapid fall in serum sodium can cause cerebral oedema, seizures, coma and death.

| Severity | Serum sodium
| Mild | 130–134 mmol/L
| Moderate | 125–129 mmol/L
| Profound/severe biochemical hyponatraemia| <125 mmol/L

blocks.text: **A. Hypovolaemic** **hyponatraemia**
Occurs when sodium and water are lost, but sodium loss is proportionally greater.
**B. Euvolaemic** **hyponatraemia**
Occurs when total body water increases without obvious peripheral oedema.

items.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH).

blocks.text: **C. Hypervolaemic** **hyponatraemia**
Occurs when both sodium and water are retained, but water retention is proportionally greater.

blocks.title: The objectives of hyponatraemia management are:

items.text: Stabilise patients with seizures, coma or severe neurological manifestations.
Avoid excessive or overly rapid sodium correction.
Identify and treat the underlying cause.
Correct associated fluid and electrolyte abnormalities.
Establish an appropriate long-term fluid and medication plan.

PRIORITY 1
**Treat severe neurological symptoms**

**4.3 Isotonic saline in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia**
First-line for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia
In hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, reduced circulating volume stimulates non-osmotic ADH secretion, causing water retention.
Restoring circulating volume suppresses this stimulus and allows the kidneys to excrete excess water.
**Adult prescription: 0.9% sodium chloride**

**4.5 Treatment of SIADH**
The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) causes excessive ADH activity, leading to water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.

blocks.text: Hyponatraemia in children requires particular caution because neurological deterioration can occur rapidly.
**A. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia**
Hypertonic saline is indicated in children with seizures, coma or severe neurological manifestations attributable to hyponatraemia.

blocks.title: A commonly used paediatric emergency regimen is:

items.text: Administration: Over approximately 10–20 minutes, according to the paediatric emergency protocol.
Repeat if severe symptoms persist, with reassessment of serum sodium.
Initial treatment target: Increase sodium by approximately 4–6 mmol/L.

blocks.text: **B. Hypovolaemic** **hyponatraemia**

items.text: Administer according to the child's circulatory status.
Use smaller, carefully reassessed volumes in children with cardiac or renal disease.

blocks.text: **C. Maintenance fluid**
Once circulation is restored, use an appropriate isotonic maintenance fluid when IV maintenance is required, with individualised electrolyte and fluid calculations.
Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids in children at risk of hospital-acquired hyponatraemia.
**D. SIADH**

items.text: Restrict fluid under paediatric specialist guidance.
Avoid routine use of adult tolvaptan regimens in children.

blocks.text: Major complication of rapid sodium correction
Osmotic demyelination syndrome occurs when chronic hyponatraemia is corrected too rapidly, resulting in injury to myelin in the central nervous system.
The classical lesion is central pontine myelinolysis, although demyelination can also occur outside the pons.

items.text: Very low initial serum sodium, particularly ≤105 mmol/L.

items.text: Initial emergency correction of 4–6 mmol/L in severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is intended to relieve cerebral oedema.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. High-yield clinical pearls and examination points

blocks.text: **20 essential facts**

items.text: Hyponatraemia is serum sodium below 135 mmol/L.
Hypotonic hyponatraemia has serum osmolality below 275 mOsm/kg.
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia commonly results from vomiting, diarrhoea and diuretics.
SIADH is an important cause of euvolaemic hyponatraemia.
Heart failure and cirrhosis commonly cause hypervolaemic hyponatraemia.
Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia requires 3% hypertonic saline.
The initial correction target is approximately 4–6 mmol/L.
Do not attempt to normalise sodium rapidly.
Chronic hyponatraemia carries a risk of osmotic demyelination.
Alcohol use disorder and malnutrition increase ODS risk.
Hypokalaemia increases the risk of ODS.
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is generally treated with 0.9% saline.
Fluid restriction is a common first-line treatment for SIADH.
Tolvaptan is not an emergency substitute for hypertonic saline.
Adrenal insufficiency is an important reversible cause.
Potassium replacement can contribute to sodium correction.
Sudden water diuresis can cause unexpected overcorrection.
Desmopressin and 5% glucose can be used in selected overcorrection rescue protocols.
**E – Euvolaemic:** No obvious extracellular fluid overload or depletion.
**V – Hypervolaemic:** Excess fluid with oedema or congestion.
**F – Fluid restriction:** Many cases of SIADH and hypervolaemic hyponatraemia.
